sections.title: Problem-Solving Tools
sections.summary: Quality managers must master the 7 classic quality tools, the 7 management & planning tools, the structured problem-solving model (PDCA/DMAIC/Kepner-Tregoe), creativity techniques (Six Hats, SCAMPER, TRIZ), and Cost of Quality (P-A-F-F). Common failure mode: jumping to solutions before validating root cause.

concepts.definition: (1) Flowchart, (2) Check Sheet (tally sheet), (3) Cause-and-Effect / Ishikawa / Fishbone diagram, (4) Pareto Chart, (5) Control Chart, (6) Histogram, (7) Scatter Diagram.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 7 in order. Each maps to a phase of investigation.

concepts.definition: Fishbone diagram organizing potential causes by category. Manufacturing: 4Ms (Manpower, Machinery, Methods, Materials). Service: 4Ps (People, Policies, Procedures, Plant).
concepts.examTip: Manufacturing → 4Ms; Service → 4Ps. Created by Ishikawa.

concepts.definition: 80% of effects come from 20% of causes (Vilfredo Pareto, applied broadly by Juran). Pareto chart arranges bars by descending frequency with a cumulative percentage line.
concepts.examTip: Not all problems have a Pareto shape — sometimes bars are nearly equal.

concepts.definition: Statistical measure of linear association between two variables. r approaches +1 (strong positive), -1 (strong negative), or 0 (no correlation). Visual slope is NOT a measure of correlation strength.
concepts.examTip: Correlation ≠ causation. Visual slope can mislead — calculate r.

concepts.definition: (1) Activity Network Diagram (AND), (2) Affinity Diagram, (3) Interrelationship Digraph, (4) Matrix Diagram, (5) Prioritization Matrix, (6) Process Decision Program Chart (PDPC), (7) Tree Diagram.
concepts.examTip: Different from the 7 classic tools. Used for planning and complex decision-making.

concepts.definition: Method to organize a large group of brainstormed ideas into natural categories using sticky notes. Creates jointly built mental model.
concepts.examTip: Affinity = group/sort. Used after brainstorming.

concepts.definition: Maps cause-and-effect relationships between ideas using arrows. Counting 'arrows in' vs 'arrows out' identifies primary drivers (out > in) and outcomes (in > out).
concepts.examTip: Identifies leverage points — focus on primary drivers.

concepts.definition: Identifies what could go wrong in a project, contingency plans, and resource availability. Similar to fault tree analysis applied to project planning.
concepts.examTip: PDPC = anticipate failures and plan contingencies.

concepts.definition: (1) Identify the problem, (2) List possible root causes, (3) Search out the most likely root cause, (4) Identify potential solutions, (5) Select and implement, (6) Follow up to evaluate, (7) Standardize the process.
concepts.examTip: Step 7 (standardize) prevents regression. Often skipped in real projects.

concepts.definition: Plan-Do-Check-Act (Shewhart, popularized by Deming who later promoted Plan-Do-Study-Act). Foundation of continuous improvement.
concepts.examTip: Shewhart created it; Deming preferred PDSA (Study emphasizes learning over checking).
definitionBullets: **Plan** — identify problem, analyze, set objectives, plan changes
**Do** — implement on small scale, collect data
**Check** (or **Study** in PDSA) — compare results to objectives
**Act** — standardize if good, or adjust and repeat cycle

concepts.definition: Fact-based root cause analysis (Rand Corp., 1950s). Four steps: (1) Problem Analysis, (2) Decision Analysis, (3) Situation Appraisal, (4) Potential Problem Analysis.
concepts.examTip: Kepner-Tregoe is structured and rational — focuses on systematically eliminating possibilities.

concepts.definition: Define (charter, VOC), Measure (current process, MSA), Analyze (root causes), Improve (design future state, implement), Control (control plan, SPC, sustain).
concepts.examTip: Memorize DMAIC phases and key tools per phase.
6σ = 3.4 DPMO. Memorize.

concepts.definition: Systematic identification of potential failures, their effects, and preventive/corrective actions. DFMEA = product/design; PFMEA = process. Computes RPN to prioritize.
concepts.examTip: Each scale 1–10. RPN > threshold (often 100 or 125) triggers action.

concepts.definition: Iterative root cause technique — ask 'Why?' approximately 5 times to drill from symptom to root cause. Simple but powerful.
concepts.examTip: Best for non-complex problems. Combine with fishbone for complex ones.

concepts.definition: Generate → Discuss/refine → Add/delete/combine/modify → Select and verify feasible ideas. Quantity over quality in generation phase.
concepts.examTip: Defer judgment in idea generation. Evaluate later.

concepts.definition: White (facts), Red (emotions), Black (negative/risks), Yellow (positive/optimism), Green (creative/alternatives), Blue (process/control).
concepts.examTip: All team members wear the same hat at the same time. Forces parallel perspectives.

concepts.definition: Creativity prompts: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse/Rearrange.
concepts.examTip: SCAMPER spurs ideation by forcing perspective shifts.

concepts.definition: Russian acronym for 'Theory of Inventive Problem-Solving.' 40 inventive principles enabling systematic innovation. Allows average inventors to access patterns from breakthrough inventions.
concepts.examTip: TRIZ = systematic creativity using 40 principles.

concepts.definition: Structured ranking and voting to narrow many ideas to a few. Multiple rounds with elimination of low-vote items.
concepts.examTip: NGT/multivoting = democratic narrowing without dominant voices controlling.

concepts.definition: Prevention (training, planning, audits), Appraisal (testing, inspection, calibration), Internal Failure (rework, scrap before delivery), External Failure (warranty, returns, lawsuits after delivery).
concepts.examTip: Goal: shift spending TO Prevention, AWAY from failures. Total COQ DECREASES.
definitionBullets: **Appraisal** — inspection and testing to detect defects
**Internal failure** — defects caught before shipment (scrap, rework)

concepts.definition: Investing in Prevention reduces all downstream failure costs. External failures are MOST expensive; Prevention is CHEAPEST. Typical organization starts with 60–70% in failure costs and aims to flip toward prevention.
concepts.examTip: 1-10-100 rule: $1 prevention = $10 appraisal = $100 failure.

concepts.definition: Concurrent product/process design to prevent defects, simplify production, and reduce parts count.
concepts.examTip: DFMA reduces parts. Fewer parts = less to fail.

concepts.definition: Adds statistical techniques (DOE, tolerance design) to DFMA. Builds quality into the design rather than inspecting it later. Often uses DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify).
concepts.examTip: DFSS = upstream Six Sigma. DMADV is the design-side counterpart to DMAIC.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the 7 classic tools BEST shows the relationship between two variables?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A scatter diagram plots one variable against another to reveal correlation. Histogram shows distribution; Pareto ranks; control chart monitors over time.

practiceQuestions.q: An RPN calculation gives Severity=9, Occurrence=4, Detection=3. The RPN is:
At Six Sigma quality level, defects per million opportunities are approximately:
An organization has Total COQ = 15% of sales, with 45% in internal failure, 30% in external failure, 20% appraisal, and 5% prevention. The BEST first action is:
options: Increase prevention investment to reduce both internal and external failure
Accept the current distribution as normal
Outsource quality to a third party
practiceQuestions.explanation: Increasing prevention reduces all downstream failures. With 75% of COQ in failures, prevention investment yields the highest leverage.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the 7 management & planning tools is BEST suited to organizing brainstormed ideas into natural categories?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Affinity diagrams group ideas by natural similarity using sticky notes. Tree diagrams decompose hierarchically; matrices compare; prioritization weights alternatives.

flashcards.back: Flowchart, Check sheet, Cause-and-Effect, Pareto, Control chart, Histogram, Scatter diagram.
AND, Affinity, Interrelationship digraph, Matrix, Prioritization matrix, PDPC, Tree.
4Ms (Manufacturing): Manpower, Machinery, Methods, Materials. 4Ps (Service): People, Policies, Procedures, Plant.
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.
RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection (each 1–10 scale).
3.4 defects per million opportunities.
Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure.
Problem Analysis, Decision Analysis, Situation Appraisal, Potential Problem Analysis.
White (facts), Red (emotions), Black (negative), Yellow (positive), Green (creative), Blue (control).
Theory of Inventive Problem-Solving — 40 principles for systematic innovation.

summaryBullets: **7 Classic QC Tools** (Ishikawa): Cause-effect, Check sheet, Control chart, Histogram, Pareto, Scatter, Stratification/Flowchart
**7 Management & Planning Tools** (newer): Affinity, Interrelationship digraph, Tree, Matrix, Prioritization matrix, PDPC, Activity network
**Pareto Principle**: 80/20 — focus on the vital few causes producing most defects
**PDCA/PDSA cycle**: Plan → Do → Check (or Study) → Act — Deming/Shewhart
**DMAIC** (Six Sigma): Define → Measure → Analyze → Improve → Control
**5 Whys** = root cause via iterative questioning; **FMEA** = forward-looking risk
**Six Sigma** = 3.4 DPMO; **3σ** = 66,800 DPMO. Big gap.
**COQ** = Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure

sections.title: Process Management
sections.summary: A process is a series of interrelated actions transforming inputs into outputs. Process management uses SIPOC, mapping, documentation hierarchies, lean tools (5S, JIT, Kanban, VSM, SMED, Poka-Yoke, Kaizen, OEE), and Theory of Constraints to systematically improve flow, eliminate waste, and reduce variation.

concepts.definition: A series of interrelated actions that transform a concept, request, or order into a delivered product or service. Adds value to inputs and provides outputs to internal/external customers.
concepts.examTip: Every process must add value — otherwise it is waste.

concepts.definition: Suppliers → Inputs → Process → Outputs → Customers. Foundational tool for understanding any process from a management perspective. Used in Six Sigma Define phase.
concepts.examTip: SIPOC is THE first map you draw to understand a process.

concepts.definition: Oval = terminal (start/end); Rectangle = activity; Diamond = decision; Arrow = flow line; D-shape = delay/wait; Document shape = input/output; Circle with letter = page link.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all standard symbols. Decision diamond branches based on yes/no question.

concepts.definition: Grid-format process map with departments in columns. Shows handoffs and where work crosses functional boundaries — a primary source of disconnects.
concepts.examTip: Swim lanes reveal cross-functional handoffs and accountability gaps.

concepts.definition: (1) Quality Manual (What/Why), (2) Procedures (Who/What/When), (3) Work Instructions (How), (4) Records (objective evidence/data).
concepts.examTip: 4-level pyramid. Quality Manual at top; Records at bottom.

concepts.definition: Document defining product/process characteristics, tolerances, measurements, controls, and reaction plans. Supports — does not replace — work instructions.
concepts.examTip: Control plan = systematic capture of how each characteristic is monitored.

concepts.term: Automotive APQP / PPAP / FMEA / MSA / SPC
concepts.definition: APQP: Advanced Product Quality Planning (5-phase product development). PPAP: Production Part Approval Process (documents launch readiness). FMEA: failure mode analysis. MSA: measurement system analysis. SPC: statistical process control. All required by IATF 16949.
concepts.examTip: These five tools form the core of automotive QMS expectations.

concepts.definition: Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects. Some add an 8th: unused human talent.
concepts.examTip: TIMWOOD acronym. Be ready to classify any example into one of the seven.
definitionBullets: **I**nventory — excess raw, WIP, or finished goods

concepts.definition: Sort (Seiri — separate needed from unneeded; red tags), Set in Order (Seiton — neat arrangement), Shine (Seiso — clean), Standardize (Seiketsu — maintain), Sustain (Shitsuke — habituate).
concepts.examTip: Memorize order: Sort → Set → Shine → Standardize → Sustain. Some add 6th 'S' for Safety.

concepts.definition: Status of process understood at-a-glance — color codes, andon lights, signage, tool boards. Cuts costs, improves communication, identifies safety hazards, enables rapid correction.
concepts.examTip: Visual management is core to Lean — see the abnormality immediately.

concepts.definition: Material delivered exactly when needed. Originally Ford 'dock to factory floor,' refined by Taiichi Ohno into Toyota Production System. Pull-driven, not forecast-driven.
concepts.examTip: JIT = pull system. Reduces inventory, surfaces defects faster.

concepts.definition: Average WIP = Throughput Rate × Average Lead Time. Foundation of JIT and flow analysis.
concepts.examTip: Reduce WIP → must reduce throughput or lead time. Memorize the formula.

concepts.definition: Pull signal (originally cards) authorizing upstream production or material movement based on downstream consumption. Enables JIT.
concepts.formula: Min Kanban Quantity = (Demand during Lead Time + Safety Stock) / Container Quantity
concepts.examTip: Kanban PULLS, doesn't push. Goal is one-piece flow.

concepts.definition: Charts all material and information flow from raw material to customer. Three types: Material flow (manufacturing), Transactional (TVSM — non-mfg processes), Enterprise (EVSM — across business). Two states: Current State, Future State.
concepts.formula: Takt Time = Available Work Time ÷ Customer Demand
concepts.examTip: Always map current state first, then future state. Never improve the future without seeing the current.

concepts.definition: Shigeo Shingo's method to reduce setup/changeover time. Key step: convert internal setup (machine stopped) to external setup (machine running). Goal: under 10 minutes.
concepts.examTip: Internal → external is the key conversion. Enables small batch production.

concepts.definition: Shigeo Shingo's mistake-prevention approach. Two systems: Control (prevents error) and Warning (alerts operator). Three device types: Contact, Counting, Motion sequence.
concepts.examTip: Control approach is preferred — it prevents the error completely.

concepts.definition: (1) Information errors — incorrect/ambiguous/missing/inadequate warning; (2) Omission/Commission — wrong addition or harmful action; (3) Selection errors — wrong part/destination; (4) Misalignment — misuse or rush.
concepts.examTip: Match scenarios to one of these four mistake categories.

concepts.definition: Intense 3–5 day rapid improvement event. Cross-functional team focused on a target process. Typical Mon-train, Tue-current state, Wed-future state, Thu-data, Fri-implement.
concepts.examTip: Kaizen blitz = focused rapid improvement. Different from continuous kaizen philosophy.

concepts.definition: Measure of equipment efficiency combining three components.
concepts.examTip: World-class OEE ≈ 85%. Memorize the formula.

concepts.definition: Systems-thinking methodology. Performance is constrained by the weakest link. Goal: identify and exploit constraints to maximize throughput.
concepts.examTip: Goldratt's 'The Goal' is the foundational text. TOC ≠ Pareto — focuses on one constraint at a time.

concepts.definition: (1) Identify the constraint, (2) Exploit the constraint (squeeze more capacity without major changes), (3) Subordinate everything else to the constraint, (4) Elevate the constraint (major changes if needed), (5) Repeat — don't let inertia become the new constraint.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 5 steps. Step 5 is critical — TOC is iterative.

concepts.definition: Throughput (T): rate at which system generates money via sales. Inventory (I): money tied up in things to sell. Operating Expense (OE): money spent turning inventory into throughput.
concepts.formula: Productivity = T/OE | Profit = T − OE | ROI = (T − OE)/I
concepts.examTip: Memorize T, I, OE. Throughput goes up; Inventory and OE go down.

concepts.definition: Physical constraints: easier to identify (raw materials, equipment, workforce). Policy constraints: harder — rules, procedures, management decisions limiting throughput. Eliminating policy constraints yields bigger gains.
concepts.examTip: Most real constraints are POLICY, not physical.

practiceQuestions.q: In a SIPOC analysis, the 'P' represents:
practiceQuestions.explanation: SIPOC = Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the seven wastes is BEST illustrated by 'producing more than the customer ordered to keep machines busy'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Overproduction is producing more than current demand. It cascades into other wastes (excess inventory, longer lead times).
Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. (Some practitioners add Safety as a 6th S.)

practiceQuestions.q: In SMED, the goal is to convert:
options: External setup steps to internal setup steps
Internal setup steps to external setup steps
All setup steps to automatic operation
practiceQuestions.explanation: Internal setup happens while the machine is stopped — the key is to move as much as possible to external (while machine is still running).

practiceQuestions.q: OEE of a machine: Availability=80%, Performance=90%, Quality=95%. OEE equals:
In Goldratt's Theory of Constraints, the second focusing step is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: After identifying, the next step is to EXPLOIT — squeeze more capacity from the constraint without major investment, before subordinating or elevating.

Quality Manual → Procedures → Work Instructions → Records.

Available Work Time ÷ Customer Demand.

summaryBullets: **SIPOC** = Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers — high-level process map
**QMS Documentation 4 levels**: Manual → Procedures → Work Instructions → Records
**7 Wastes (TIMWOOD)**: Transport, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overprocessing, Overproduction, Defects (some add 8th = Skills)
**5S**: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain
**Just-in-Time (JIT)** + **Kanban** + **Value Stream Mapping** = Lean foundation
**Poka-yoke** = mistake-proofing; 4 mistake categories: information, misalignment, omission, sequence
**OEE** = Availability × Performance × Quality (target: 85%+ world-class)
**Theory of Constraints (TOC)** — focus on bottleneck; 5 focusing steps

sections.title: Measurement, Assessment, and Metrics
sections.summary: Statistics turns data into information. Quality managers must apply sampling, descriptive statistics, distributions, SPC, MSA (gage R&R, accuracy/precision), trend and pattern analysis, and process capability indices (Cp/Cpk/Pp/Ppk) — and distinguish common from special cause variation. Reliability is captured through MTTF/MTBF/MTTR and the bathtub curve.

concepts.definition: Three-level measurement model: Goal (conceptual), Question (operational, defines what to measure), Metric (quantitative answer to the question).
concepts.examTip: GQM ensures every metric ties back to a goal — no orphan measurements.

concepts.definition: (1) Never measure without knowing who supplies data, who consumes information, and the cost-effectiveness; (2) Always involve the people doing the work; (3) The primary reason is to IMPROVE — not control or punish.
concepts.examTip: Metrics are for improvement, not surveillance.

concepts.definition: Random (every item has equal chance), Stratified (every nth item from subgroup), Cluster (random subgroup, all items examined). Choice depends on purpose and cost.
concepts.examTip: Stratified sampling protects against bias when subgroups differ. Random sampling is gold standard.

concepts.definition: Alpha = Producer's Risk = probability of rejecting good product (Type I error). Beta = Consumer's Risk = probability of accepting bad product (Type II error). Typical: α = 0.05, β = 0.10.
concepts.examTip: α = Type I = reject GOOD. β = Type II = accept BAD.
definitionBullets: **Alpha (α)** — Type I — Producer's risk — REJECTING a good lot (false alarm)
**Beta (β)** — Type II — Consumer's risk — ACCEPTING a bad lot (miss)

concepts.definition: AQL (Acceptable Quality Limit): worst tolerable process average submitted for acceptance. LTPD (Lot Tolerance Percent Defective): the point on OC curve associated with consumer's risk. Defined in ANSI/ASQ Z1.4.
concepts.examTip: AQL ≠ acceptable quality. It's the worst the customer will tolerate, not the goal.

concepts.definition: Single: one sample, accept if ≤ c defects. Double: two samples; first determines accept/reject/test more. Multiple: up to 7 sequential samples — most discriminating but susceptible to abuse.
concepts.examTip: Sampling complexity vs. cost trade-off. ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 governs in many industries.

concepts.definition: Mean (average): ΣX ÷ n. Median: middle value when sorted (or avg of two middles for even n). Mode: most frequently occurring value.
concepts.examTip: Median is robust to outliers; mean is not. Mode may not be unique.

concepts.definition: Range (R): max − min. Variance: average of squared deviations. Standard Deviation (s): square root of variance.
concepts.examTip: Sample SD divides by (n − 1); population SD by N.

concepts.definition: Normal (bell-shaped, symmetric), Exponential (time between events), Weibull (reliability — bathtub), Poisson (rare events in n trials, p < 0.10), Binomial (yes/no in n trials), Hypergeometric (without replacement).
concepts.examTip: Normal for continuous data, Poisson for rare counts, Binomial for pass/fail.

concepts.definition: Method using control charts to determine if a process is stable (predictable) and detect special-cause variation early. Based on Shewhart's framework.
concepts.examTip: SPC is the foundation of variables-based quality control.

concepts.definition: X̄-R (subgroup average + range), X̄-s (average + standard deviation, larger subgroups), CUSUM (cumulative sum, detects small shifts), individuals (X-MR for individual measurements).
concepts.examTip: Variables data → X̄-R or X̄-s. Use s when subgroup size > ~10.

concepts.definition: p-chart (fraction defective, variable n), np-chart (number defective, constant n), c-chart (count of defects, constant area), u-chart (defects per unit, variable area).
concepts.examTip: p/np for defectives; c/u for defects. Constant n → np or c; variable n → p or u.

concepts.term: Four Control Chart Criteria for In-Control
concepts.definition: (1) No visible pattern; (2) Approximately equal points above and below centerline; (3) Some points close to control limits but not beyond; (4) Approximately two-thirds of points within ±1σ.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all four criteria for an in-control process.

concepts.definition: Repeatability: variation in same gage with same operator measuring the same part repeatedly (gage variation). Reproducibility: variation between operators using same gage on same part (operator variation). Together = Gage R&R.
concepts.examTip: Repeat = same operator/gage. Reproduce = different operators/same gage.

concepts.term: Accuracy vs Precision vs Bias vs Linearity
concepts.definition: Accuracy: closeness to true value (validity). Precision: repeatability (reliability). Bias: systematic difference between observed average and reference. Linearity: consistency of bias across the measurement range.
concepts.examTip: Target analogy: Tight cluster off-center = precise but not accurate. Centered scatter = accurate but not precise. Tight + centered = both.

concepts.definition: Comparing instrument readings to a traceable standard (e.g., NIST). Each device gets ID, calibration frequency, and method. Record as-found and after-corrected conditions.
concepts.examTip: Calibration is traceable to a national/international standard.

concepts.definition: Common (chance) cause: inherent random variation always present in a stable process. Special (assignable) cause: detectable, removable variation from a specific source — appears as out-of-control patterns.
concepts.examTip: Stable process = common cause only. Out-of-control = special cause to investigate.

concepts.definition: Overcorrecting a stable process treating common-cause variation as special-cause. Increases variation rather than reducing it. Deming's funnel experiment demonstrated this.
concepts.examTip: Tampering MAKES IT WORSE. Don't react to every fluctuation in a stable process.

concepts.definition: Sporadic: sudden departure from normal — restore control. Chronic: ongoing baseline that needs breakthrough improvement, not just control.
concepts.examTip: Sporadic = control. Chronic = breakthrough.

concepts.definition: Ratio of specification range to process spread. Measures POTENTIAL capability assuming the process is centered.
concepts.examTip: Cp > 1.33 = capable. Cp = 2 → 6σ short-term.

concepts.definition: Accounts for centering. Smaller of (USL − X̄)/3σ and (X̄ − LSL)/3σ.
concepts.examTip: Cpk ≤ Cp. If Cpk = Cp, process is perfectly centered.

concepts.definition: Same formulas as Cp/Cpk but use overall (long-term) standard deviation instead of within-subgroup standard deviation. Used for initial / new-product capability studies.
concepts.examTip: Pp/Ppk = long-term performance. Cp/Cpk = short-term capability.

concepts.definition: Cp/Cpk > 1.33: capable. Cp/Cpk = 1.00–1.33: capable with tight control. Cp/Cpk < 1.00: not capable. Ppk > 1.67: capable (long-term).
concepts.examTip: 1.33 (short-term) and 1.67 (long-term) are the magic numbers.

concepts.definition: Failure rate vs time has three phases: (1) Infant Mortality (decreasing rate — defects burn-in), (2) Useful Life (constant random failure rate), (3) Wear-out (increasing failure rate — end of life).
concepts.examTip: Most modeling assumes the constant-rate useful-life region. Burn-in screens infant mortality.

concepts.definition: MTTF: Mean Time To Failure (nonrepairable items). MTBF: Mean Time Between Failures (repairable items). MTTR: Mean Time To Repair.
concepts.examTip: MTTF = nonrepairable; MTBF = repairable. Don't confuse them.
definitionBullets: **MTTF** — Mean Time To Failure — non-repairable items (light bulbs)
**MTBF** — Mean Time Between Failures — repairable items (machines)
**MTTR** — Mean Time To Repair — how fast you recover

concepts.definition: Operational availability — combines reliability and maintainability.
concepts.examTip: Improve availability by raising MTBF or lowering MTTR.

keyFigures: Walter Shewhart (SPC, common vs special cause)
W. Edwards Deming (funnel experiment, profound knowledge)

practiceQuestions.q: In sampling, alpha (α) risk is BEST described as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alpha (Producer's Risk / Type I) is the probability of rejecting good product. Beta is Type II (accepting bad).

practiceQuestions.q: A process has Cp = 1.50 and Cpk = 0.90. This indicates:
options: The process is incapable and uncentered
The process is capable and centered
The process has potential capability but is off-center
The process is in statistical control
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cp = 1.50 indicates good potential. Cpk = 0.90 < Cp shows the process is shifted off-center. Centering improvement could realize Cp.

practiceQuestions.q: Which control chart is BEST for tracking the count of defects in a constant-size sample?
practiceQuestions.explanation: c-chart counts defects per constant inspection unit. np-chart counts DEFECTIVES (not defects). u-chart is for variable sample size.

practiceQuestions.q: Repeatability in a Gage R&R study refers to:
options: Variation in same operator using same gage on same part
practiceQuestions.explanation: Repeatability is gage variation when same operator measures same part repeatedly. Reproducibility is variation BETWEEN operators.

practiceQuestions.q: MTBF = 200 hours and MTTR = 5 hours. Operational availability is approximately:
Treating common-cause variation as if it were special-cause and adjusting the process is called:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tampering — overcorrecting a stable process — increases variation. Demonstrated by Deming's funnel experiment.

flashcards.back: α = Producer's risk = reject GOOD (Type I). β = Consumer's risk = accept BAD (Type II).
Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ.
Cpk = min[(USL − X̄)/3σ, (X̄ − LSL)/3σ].
> 1.33 (short-term). > 1.67 (long-term Ppk).
Repeatability = same operator/same gage. Reproducibility = different operators/same gage.
Infant mortality → Useful life (constant rate) → Wear-out.
MTTF = nonrepairable. MTBF = repairable.
Ao = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR).
Common = inherent random. Special = assignable, detectable, removable.
Overcorrecting common-cause variation; increases overall variation.

summaryBullets: **GQM** = Goal-Question-Metric — start with the goal, derive metrics
**Alpha (α)** = Type I = producer's risk = false alarm; **Beta (β)** = Type II = consumer's risk = miss
**AQL** = Acceptable Quality Limit (good lots accepted); **LTPD** = Lot Tolerance % Defective (bad lots rejected)
**Central tendency**: mean, median, mode | **Dispersion**: range, variance, std dev
**SPC**: variables charts (X̄-R, X̄-s, I-MR) for measurements; attributes (p, np, c, u) for counts
**Cp** = process capability (centered); **Cpk** = capability adjusted for centering
**Cpk thresholds**: <1.0 not capable | 1.33 standard | 1.67 high-volume/safety-critical
**Common cause** = inherent variation (don't tamper); **Special cause** = assignable (investigate)
**Bathtub curve**: infant mortality → useful life → wear-out failure
